blocks.text: Just as among birds too the ossifrages have a constant love for their chicks, and the doves with their heavy moaning. That ravens, too, hate their chicks, though very many assert it, is nevertheless a fiction, as was amply proved above ^{a)}; and the eagle ^{b)} casts one egg or chick out of its nest for no other reason than that it is unequal to feeding and warming them all. But that the ostrich not infrequently leaves its eggs on the ground and neglects them, although the Greek and Roman writers, to whom the nature of this animal was not sufficiently known, do not report it, is nevertheless quite certain to me from the records of the Arabs. Damir: وهي تخرج لطلب الطعم فمتي وجدت بيض نعامة اخري تحضنه وتنسي بيضها ولعلها ان تصاد فلا ترجع اليه ولهذا توصف بالحمق ويضرب بها المثل في ذلك [wa-hiya takhruju li-ṭalab al-ṭuʿm fa-matī wajadat bayḍ naʿāma ukhrī taḥḍunuhu wa-tansī bayḍahā wa-laʿallahā an tuṣād fa-lā tarjiʿ ilayhi wa-li-hādhā tūṣaf bi-l-ḥumq wa-yuḍrab bihā al-mathal fī dhālika] When it goes out of [col. 252] the nest to seek food, if it finds the egg of another ostrich, it sits on it and forgets its own; and, driven away from there by hunters, it never returns. Hence it is described as foolish, and the proverb strikes it on this account ^{(2)}. Namely احمق نعامة [aḥmaq naʿāma] More foolish than an ostrich, which the same author explains in the section On Proverbs. And the Arabs designate each of these things by proper names. بيضة [bayḍa] in general is egg, as in Hebrew ביצה, with the same letters. Hence here the plural with the suffix, ביציה, its eggs. Why an egg is so called is hidden from the Hebrews, but the Arabs derive it from whiteness. For with them the verb باض [bāḍa] means to be white. But the ostrich's egg is called by a special name تومة [tūma] thauma, which in Greek means marvel. And تريكة [tarīka] tharicha, when the chick has come out of it. And نتل [natl] nethel, when it has been left by the male, or بيضة البلد [bayḍat al-balad] egg of the region. Alcamus: تومة بيضة النعام [tūma bayḍat al-naʿām] Thauma, the ostrich's egg. التريكة البيضة بعد [II, 857] ان يخرج منه الفرخ ويخص بالنعام [al-tarīka al-bayḍa baʿda an yakhruja minhu al-farkh wa-yakhuṣṣu bi-l-naʿām] Tharicha, an egg after the chick has come out of it; but it is said properly of the ostrich. النتل بيضة النعام يملا ماء فيدفن في المفازة [al-natl bayḍat al-naʿām yumlaʾ māʾan fa-yudfan fī al-mafāza] Nethel, an ostrich egg full of water, which is buried in the desert, that is, in the midst of the sands. And elsewhere: هو اذل من بيضة البلد اي من بيضة النعام التي تركها [huwa adhallu min bayḍat al-balad ay min bayḍat al-naʿām allatī tarakathā] He is more worthless than the egg of the region, that is, than the ostrich's egg, which it has abandoned. The ostrich's nest, in which such eggs are usually found, is called ادحي [udḥī] udcha, ادحوة [udḥuwwa] udchua, and ادحية [udḥiyya] udchia, on account of the sand spread out all around. For دحا [daḥā] is to spread out. The same Alcamus: الادحي والادحوة والادحية مبيض النعام في الرمل [al-udḥī wa-l-udḥuwwa wa-l-udḥiyya mabīḍ al-naʿām fī al-raml] Udcha, and udchua, and udchia, the ostrich's nest in the sands. Of which Philes says thus in his Iambics:
Καὶ τὴν καλιὰν τοῖς ποσὶν διαγλύφειν Εἰς ἀνέχουσαν ψάμμον ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, [Kai tēn kalian tois posin diaglyphein Eis anechousan psammon en tō dapedō,]

And (they say) that it hollows out its nest with its feet upon raised sand on the ground. But much more fully Aelian, from whom this was adapted, book 14, chapter 7: Καλιὰν ἐργάζεται ταπεινὴν ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, τὴν ψάμμον διαγλύψασα τοῖς ποσὶ, καὶ τὸ μὲν μεσαίτατον αὐτῆς κοῖλόν ἐστι· τὰ χείλη δὲ τὰ κύκλῳ ὑψηλὰ ἐργάζεται, ἀποτειχίζουσα τρόπον τινά· ἵνα τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕδωρ ἀποστέξῃ, καὶ μὴ εἰσρέῃ τῇ καλιᾷ, καὶ ἐπικλύζῃ τῆς στρουθοῦ τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ὄντας ἁπαλούς. [Kalian ergazetai tapeinēn en tō dapedō, tēn psammon diaglypsasa tois posi, kai to men mesaitaton autēs koilon estin; ta cheilē de ta kyklō hypsēla ergazetai, apoteichizousa tropon tina; hina to ek Dios hydōr apostexē, kai mē eisreē tē kalia, kai epiklyzē tēs strouthou tous neottous, ontas hapalous.] It builds a low nest on the ground, hollowing out the sand with its feet. Its middle is hollow, but it raises the surrounding rims high and, as it were, walls it round, so that those rims may keep out the rain, lest it flow into the nest and wash over the ostrich's still tender chicks. So it is now not obscure why in Arabic it is called ادحي [udḥī] from the sand spread out all around. Note in passing that in Aelian's text ἀποστάξῃ [apostaxē] is wrongly read, and that the true reading is ἀποστέξῃ [apostexē], which has been relegated to the margin. But both Aelian and Philes must also be corrected in the words διαγλύψασα [diaglypsasa] and διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein]. For one should read διαγλάψασα [diaglapsasa] and διαγλάφειν [diaglaphein]. The word is taken from Homer, line 437 [col. 253] of Odyssey δ [delta], about Idothea, daughter of Proteus:
Εὐνὰς δ᾽ ἐν ψαμάθοισι διαγλάψασ᾽ ἁλίῃσιν, [Eunas d' en psamathoisi diaglaps' haliēsin,]

When she had hollowed out beds in the sands of the sea. Where the Scholiasts have: Διαγλάψασα· διακοιλάνασα [Diaglapsasa; diakoilanasa], hollowing out. But διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein] is to engrave, to carve through.
